message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"6.21","text":"Indeed, to take an immediate example (as I also said on another occasion), in the Caucasus Mountains the tomb of a certain Cronus, a man, is pointed out—the tomb of a savage tyrant and killer of his children. His son, named Zeus, became worse; appearing as ruler of the world by the power of magic, he breaks up many marriages and punishes his father together with his uncles. When he then died, the Cretans point out his tomb. In Mesopotamia there lie a certain Helios at Hatra and a certain Selene at Carrhae; in Egypt, a certain Hermes, a human being; in Thrace, Ares; in Cyprus, Aphrodite; and in Epidaurus, Asclepius. Tombs of many other such figures can also be seen.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σῆμα","chosen":"tomb","rationale":"The word can mean a sign or monument, but the burial context and the subsequent τάφον and τάφοι support “tomb.”"},{"source_quote":"κοσμοκράτωρ","chosen":"ruler of the world","rationale":"Preserves the claim of worldwide rule without importing a later technical or theological sense."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς θείοις","chosen":"his uncles","rationale":"The family and mythological context supports the substantival sense “uncles.” “The divine ones” or “gods” is lexically possible, and the phrase could instead describe companions in punishing his father."},{"source_quote":"Ἄτροις","chosen":"Hatra","rationale":"Treated as the dative plural place-name referring to Hatra in Mesopotamia."},{"source_quote":"τις ἄνθρωπος","chosen":"a certain Hermes, a human being","rationale":"The apposition explicitly identifies Hermes as human; the name is supplied by the immediately preceding Ἑρμῆς."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὕτως τελευτήσαντος","issue":"The genitive absolute does not state explicitly who died. The continuing focus and the Cretan tomb tradition favor Zeus; Cronus is grammatically possible but contextually less likely.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.22","text":"Thus it has been plainly acknowledged by those who think correctly that they were human beings. Those who were their contemporaries, perceiving that they had proved mortal, paid less attention to them after they died; but the long passage of time clothed them with the reputation of gods. Do not be amazed if those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles were deceived, or those in the days of Dionysus or anyone else of that period, since even Hector at Ilium and Achilles on the island of Leuce are worshiped by the people there, Patroclus by the Opuntians, and Alexander the Macedonian by the Rhodians.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὡμολόγηνται","chosen":"it has been plainly acknowledged","rationale":"The perfect passive reports an acknowledgment about the figures discussed in the preceding section."},{"source_quote":"ὑπαισθόμενοι","chosen":"perceiving","rationale":"The verb can express noticing, apprehending, or suspecting; “perceiving” fits their recognition of the figures’ mortality without overstating certainty."},{"source_quote":"δόξαν θεῶν","chosen":"the reputation of gods","rationale":"Δόξα here is the status, repute, or estimation attached to them, not proof that they truly became gods."},{"source_quote":"οἱ κατὰ Ἀσκληπιὸν καὶ Ἡρακλέα γενόμενοι","chosen":"those who lived in the days of Asclepius and Heracles","rationale":"The surrounding argument concerns contemporaries and the effect of elapsed time. “Those associated with Asclepius and Heracles” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"ὅπου καὶ","chosen":"since even","rationale":"Here ὅπου introduces a striking supporting circumstance rather than a literal location."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.23","text":"But among the Egyptians, even now, a man is worshiped as a god before his death. This, at least, is a lesser act of impiety, because the Egyptians accord divine honors while a man is alive; but the most ridiculous thing of all is that they worship birds and reptiles and every kind of animal. For most human beings neither understand nor do anything with judgment. Now observe what is most shameful of all: the one who, by their account, is father of gods and humans, whom most people call Zeus, they depict in a painting as a goose coupled with Leda and set up publicly. As retribution for this outrage, I would have liked it if they had portrayed their present king in a shameful coupling and, having done the same thing they have dared to do in Zeus’s case, had set it up publicly, so that, even if only through the anger of their temporary king—and he a human being—they might learn through punishment that due honor must be rendered. I tell you these things not as one who has already recognized the God who truly is, but, being fair-minded, I confess: Though I do not know what God is, still I think I know clearly that God exists.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"θείας τιμὰς νομίζουσιν","chosen":"accord divine honors","rationale":"Νομίζω can denote customary observance or acknowledgment; here it concerns treating a living person as entitled to divine honors."},{"source_quote":"δι’ αὐτῶν","chosen":"by their account","rationale":"Literally “through them.” In context it can mark Zeus’s status as established through their own representation or claim; “through their agency” remains possible."},{"source_quote":"χῆνα","chosen":"goose","rationale":"The supplied Greek explicitly says “goose,” so the familiar mythological rendering “swan” is not substituted."},{"source_quote":"πλοκῆς","chosen":"coupling","rationale":"The noun can denote entwining or entanglement; the sexual image involving Zeus and Leda supports “coupling.”"},{"source_quote":"προσκαίρου","chosen":"temporary","rationale":"The adjective emphasizes that the earthly ruler lasts only for a limited time."},{"source_quote":"τί θεὸς","chosen":"what God is","rationale":"The closing contrast is between not knowing what God is and knowing that God exists. “What sort of god” is also grammatically possible, but fits the contrast less directly."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἤθελον εἰ","issue":"The construction continuing after these words uses aorist indicatives and is compressed. It defensibly expresses an unreal wish, “I would have liked it if they had ...”; “I wanted to see whether they had ...” is grammatically conceivable but fits the argument less well. No textual correction is required.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.24","text":"To take an immediate example, the first four elements—things brought into being by another—cannot be God; neither can mixing, blending, coming-to-be, the visible vessel that encompasses the whole, the sediment collecting in Hades, the water floating on top, the boiling substance, or the air extending from it as far as the things here. For whether the four elements had stood apart from one another—in which case they could not have been mixed for the generation of a living creature without some great craftsman—or had always been joined to one another, even so they are fitted together by a craftsman mind to suit what belongs properly to the limbs and parts of the living creature, so that it can preserve the proportion of each to each, possess a well-bounded constitution, and have all its inward parts receive the appropriate harmony. Likewise, the craftsman mind precisely determines the proper places of each with complete beauty. To sum up: of all the other things that a living creature must ever have, nothing was lacking in this great living creature of the whole circuit.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὰ ὑπὸ ἄλλου γενόμενα","chosen":"things brought into being by another","rationale":"The phrase modifies the four elements and supplies the reason they cannot themselves be God."},{"source_quote":"κύτος","chosen":"vessel","rationale":"The noun denotes a hollow body, cavity, or vessel. “Vessel” preserves the cosmological container image without specifying more than the Greek does."},{"source_quote":"ὑποστάθμη","chosen":"sediment","rationale":"The noun denotes sediment, dregs, or what settles at the bottom."},{"source_quote":"ἐξ αὐτῆς","chosen":"from it","rationale":"The feminine pronoun most naturally refers to the immediately preceding “boiling substance,” though another feminine item in the list is grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὸ οἰκεῖον","chosen":"to suit what belongs properly","rationale":"The phrase indicates fitting the elements to the proper constitution or requirements of the creature’s limbs and parts."},{"source_quote":"ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον","chosen":"a well-bounded constitution","rationale":"Ἕξις here denotes condition or constitution, while εὐπερίγραφος suggests being readily circumscribed or clearly bounded. “A well-defined constitution” is also possible."},{"source_quote":"τῆς ὅλης περιφορᾶς","chosen":"of the whole circuit","rationale":"Περιφορά can denote revolution, circular motion, or a circuit. In context it characterizes the cosmos as a great living creature; “of the whole revolution” is more formally literal."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"δύνηται καὶ τὴν ἕξιν εὐπερίγραφον ἔχῃ","issue":"The singular verbs leave their subject implicit. The living creature or resulting organized whole is the best contextual referent; taking the craftsman mind as subject is less natural but grammatically conceivable.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.25","text":"Thus there must be some unoriginated craftsman mind that either gathered the elements when they were apart or, when they were together with one another, skillfully blended them for the generation of a living creature and completed a single work from them all; for it is impossible for an exceedingly wise work to be completed without some greater mind. Nor indeed can love be the craftsman of all, nor desire, nor force, nor anything else of that kind, since such things are passions and naturally come and go. Nor is anything borne along by another God, or anything altered by time or nature and dissolved into no longer existing.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀγέννητον","chosen":"unoriginated","rationale":"The adjective means not generated or not brought into being. “Unoriginated” suits the contrast with elements produced by another; “unbegotten” is possible but carries stronger traditional theological associations."},{"source_quote":"τεχνικῶς ἐκέρασεν","chosen":"skillfully blended","rationale":"The adverb emphasizes artful or craftsmanlike arrangement, while the verb describes mixing or blending."},{"source_quote":"πάνυ σοφὸν ἔργον","chosen":"an exceedingly wise work","rationale":"The phrase presents the work as embodying extraordinary wisdom or skill; “a work of surpassing skill” is an idiomatic alternative."},{"source_quote":"ἔρως","chosen":"love","rationale":"The noun can denote love as a cosmic principle and may evoke the personified Eros. Lowercase “love” avoids requiring personification."},{"source_quote":"ἅτινα πάθη ὄντα","chosen":"since such things are passions","rationale":"The relative clause classifies love, desire, force, and similar proposed principles as contingent passions."},{"source_quote":"ὑφ’ ἑτέρου φερόμενον","chosen":"borne along by another","rationale":"The passive participle can mean carried, borne, or moved by another. “Borne along” retains the concrete source image, while “moved by another” is also viable."},{"source_quote":"μηκέτι εἶναι ἀναλυόμενον","chosen":"dissolved into no longer existing","rationale":"Preserves both the image of dissolution and its stated outcome of nonexistence."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
